title: Hands-on exercises
text:
One set of exercises per session. Together they build a small practice project: a Markdown page, a report, a slide deck, and finally a published website. Use only made-up data, and your personal GitHub account for publishing.
Start by making a folder for everything: Documents/GitHub/quarto-practice/.

title: Hands-on exercises
text:
Session 1: Markdown and Quarto basics

Exercise 1: Markdown (Lesson 3, 15 min)

In quarto-practice/, create markdown-practice.qmd with a YAML header containing just a title:.
Write a short “About me” page using:

two ## headings
bold and italic text
a bulleted list and a numbered list
a link to the NV OSE training site
a table with three counties and made-up case counts, with the numbers right-aligned

Preview it.

✅ Check: everything renders formatted, and the table has three rows with right-aligned numbers.






TipShow solution





---
title: "About me"
---

## Who I am

I'm an **epidemiologist** in the *Office of State Epidemiology*.

## What I work on

- Respiratory surveillance
- Data dashboards

1. Pull the data
2. Check it
3. Report it

See the [NV OSE training site](https://nv-ose.github.io/training/).

| County | Cases |
|:-------|------:|
| Clark  |   120 |
| Washoe |    45 |
| Elko   |     6 |





Bonus: Write a README (10 min)
Download the NV OSE README template, save it as README.md in quarto-practice/, and fill in the title, description, project structure, and maintainer for your practice project. Open the preview to check it.


Exercise 2: Quarto extras (Lesson 4, 10 min)
Add to the same page:

A tip callout and a collapsed callout titled “Show answer”.
A tab set with two tabs, “Windows” and “Mac”.
A footnote.

✅ Check: the collapsed callout opens when clicked, and the tabs switch.


Exercise 3: Code (Lesson 5, 15 min)

Add this chunk, which makes a small made-up data frame:
```{r}
#| label: data
cases <- data.frame(
  county = c("Clark", "Washoe", "Elko"),
  cases  = c(120, 45, 6)
)
```
Add a chunk that shows the data as a table with knitr::kable(), with its code hidden.
Write a sentence that reports the total number of cases with inline code.

✅ Check: the page shows a table (no code) and a sentence saying “171”.






TipShow solution





```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(cases, col.names = c("County", "Cases"))
```

There were `{r} sum(cases$cases)` cases in total.

title: Hands-on exercises
text:
Session 2: Documents and presentations

Exercise 4: An HTML report (Lesson 6, 20 min)

Create ili-report.qmd from the complete report example in Lesson 6.
Render it. Find ili-report.html in your folder and open it in a browser.
Change set.seed(2026) to another number, render again, and check that the numbers in the Summary sentence change with the chart.
Add code-fold: true under html:, and render again.

✅ Check: a self-contained report with a table of contents, a numbered figure, a table, and a sentence whose numbers match the chart. With code-fold, a “Code” button appears above each chunk.


Exercise 5: A slide deck (Lesson 7, 20 min)

Create talk.qmd with format: revealjs and a title, author, and date.
Make at least four slides:

an incremental list
a two-column slide (text on one side, a list on the other)
a slide with speaker notes
a slide with the ILI chart from Exercise 4 (code hidden, with fig-alt)

Add slide-number: true and embed-resources: true.
Render, open talk.html in a browser, and try F, S, and Esc.

✅ Check: the deck has a title slide, the list appears one item at a time, and S shows your notes.






TipShow solution: YAML header





---
title: "ILI Update"
author: "Jane Smith"
date: today
format:
  revealjs:
    slide-number: true
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
---

title: Hands-on exercises
text:
Session 3: Websites and publishing

Exercise 6: Turn the folder into a website (Lesson 8, 20 min)

Create a website project in a new folder, quarto-site (see Lesson 8 for your editor).
Change the site title: in _quarto.yml.
Copy markdown-practice.qmd and ili-report.qmd from your practice folder into the site folder, and add both to the navbar.
Preview the site.

✅ Check: the navbar has Home, About, and your two pages, and each one opens.






TipReport options on a site



Inside a website, the site’s settings in _quarto.yml apply to every page. You can delete embed-resources: true from the report’s header; a site doesn’t need it.




Exercise 7: Sidebar and look (Lessons 8 and 10, 15 min)

Make a lessons/ folder with 01-welcome.qmd and 02-data.qmd, and add a docked sidebar listing them.
Switch to a light and dark theme pair with respect-user-color-scheme: true.
Add search: true, page-navigation: true, and a page-footer with your name.

✅ Check: a light/dark toggle in the navbar, a sidebar on the lesson pages, and a footer on every page.






TipShow solution: _quarto.yml





project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Jane's Practice Site"
  search: true
  page-navigation: true
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: lessons/01-welcome.qmd
        text: Lessons
      - ili-report.qmd
      - about.qmd
  sidebar:
    style: docked
    contents:
      - section: "Lessons"
        contents:
          - lessons/01-welcome.qmd
          - lessons/02-data.qmd
  page-footer:
    center: "Made by Jane Smith"

format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: flatly
      dark: darkly
    respect-user-color-scheme: true
    css: styles.css
    toc: true





Exercise 8: Publish it (Lesson 11, 20 min)

Add output-dir: docs and the .nojekyll resource to _quarto.yml, and create the .nojekyll file.
Stop the preview and run quarto render.
In GitHub Desktop, add the folder as a repository, commit, and publish it to your personal account as public.
Turn on GitHub Pages: Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → main → /docs → Save.
Open https://<your-username>.github.io/quarto-site/.
Update it: change a sentence, render, commit, and push. Confirm the live site changes (hard refresh with Ctrl + Shift + R).

✅ Check: your site is live, and your update appears.






TipSite not showing up?






404 page: check that Pages is set to main and /docs, and that docs/index.html was committed.
Page has no styling: check that .nojekyll is in docs/.
Change not showing: did you run quarto render before committing? Check that docs/ files changed in GitHub Desktop.
Still nothing: look at the repo’s Actions tab for a failed “pages build and deployment” run.






Bonus: Add your deck to the site
Copy talk.qmd into the site folder and add it to the navbar. Render and push. Your slides are now online at .../talk.html.

text: This lesson puts it all together: adding a new training to nv-ose.github.io/training.
crumbs: Lesson 12: Adding a training to the NV OSE site

title: Lesson 12: Adding a training to the NV OSE site
section: How the training repo is organized
text:
How the training repo is organized
training/
├── _quarto.yml          ← navbar and one sidebar per training
├── index.qmd            ← home page, with the table of trainings
├── README.md            ← the same table, for people browsing GitHub
├── styles.css           ← contrast fixes and screenshot highlight boxes
├── _template/           ← copy this to start a new training
├── images/<training>/   ← screenshots and images, one folder per training
├── pages/
│   ├── intro-to-github/
│   └── intro-to-quarto/
└── docs/                ← the rendered site (never edit by hand)






WarningThis repo is public



Everything in training, including branches and pull requests, can be seen by anyone. Use made-up or public data only, and keep internal details out.
crumbs: Lesson 12: Adding a training to the NV OSE site

title: Lesson 12: Adding a training to the NV OSE site
text:
Step by step

1. Get the repo and make a branch

In GitHub Desktop: File → Clone repository → nv-ose/training. Save it in Documents/GitHub/NV-OSE/. (Skip this if you already have it; just Pull origin.)
Current branch → New branch: yourname/add-<training-name>, e.g., jsmith/add-intro-to-r.



2. Copy the template
Copy the _template/ folder into pages/ and rename it with your training’s name (lowercase, hyphens):
pages/intro-to-r/
├── index.qmd            ← overview: audience, objectives, prerequisites, lesson table
└── 01-lesson-name.qmd   ← first lesson (rename it, e.g., 01-getting-started.qmd)
Delete the template’s empty data/ and slides/ folders if you don’t need them.


3. Write the pages

Fill in index.qmd: title, audience, level, duration, learning objectives, prerequisites, and a table linking to each lesson.
Write numbered lessons: 01-...qmd, 02-...qmd, and so on. Each needs a title: in its YAML header.
Put images in images/<training-name>/, and give every one fig-alt text (see Lesson 4).
Use callouts for tips and warnings, and collapsed callouts for answers.



4. Add it to the navigation
In _quarto.yml, add a navbar link and a sidebar, copying the existing entries:
website:
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: "Home"
        href: index.qmd
      - text: "Intro to Git & GitHub"
        href: pages/intro-to-github/index.qmd
      - text: "Intro to R"                         # ← new
        href: pages/intro-to-r/index.qmd          # ← new
  sidebar:
    - id: intro-to-github
      # ... existing ...
    - id: intro-to-r                               # ← new sidebar
      title: "Intro to R"
      style: docked
      contents:
        - href: pages/intro-to-r/index.qmd
          text: "Overview"
        - section: "Lessons"
          contents:
            - pages/intro-to-r/01-getting-started.qmd
            - pages/intro-to-r/02-importing-data.qmd


5. List it on the home page
Add a row to the Trainings table in both index.qmd (the site) and README.md (GitHub):
| [Introduction to R](pages/intro-to-r/index.qmd) | Importing data, summaries, and basic charts | Beginner | About 2 hours |


6. Preview, then render

Run quarto preview and click through every page: links, images, tabs, callouts, in light and dark mode.
Stop the preview, then run quarto render.
Fix any errors or warnings (Lesson 9).



7. Commit, push, and open a pull request

In GitHub Desktop, review the Changes list: your new pages, _quarto.yml, index.qmd, README.md, images, and the updated docs/ files. No data files, nothing internal.
Commit, e.g., Add Intro to R training.
Click Publish branch, then Create Pull Request. Add Max or Jordan as a reviewer.
After it’s approved and merged, the site updates within a couple of minutes.
crumbs: Lesson 12: Adding a training to the NV OSE site

title: Lesson 12: Adding a training to the NV OSE site
text:
Review checklist
Before you open the pull request:

Every page has a title:, and lessons are numbered in order
Overview page has audience, objectives, prerequisites, and a lesson table
Every image has fig-alt text, and no unwanted captions
Only made-up or public data; no internal servers, names, or credentials
New training is in the navbar, has a sidebar, and is listed in index.qmd and README.md
Previewed in light and dark mode; all links work
Rendered, and docs/ changes are included in the commit

title: Lesson 10: Customizing and accessibility
text: All of these settings go in _quarto.yml. After changing them, preview to see the result.

title: Lesson 10: Customizing and accessibility
section: Themes, and light and dark mode
text:
Themes, and light and dark mode
Quarto includes about two dozen free Bootswatch themes: cosmo, flatly, litera, lumen, sandstone, yeti, and more.
format:
  html:
    theme: flatly
To offer a light and a dark version, with a toggle in the navbar:
format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: cosmo
      dark: darkly
    respect-user-color-scheme: true   # start in the reader's system setting
This is what the NV OSE training site uses.

title: Lesson 10: Customizing and accessibility
text:
Logo, footer, and search
website:
  title: "My Practice Site"
  search: true                      # search box in the navbar
  page-navigation: true             # "previous / next" buttons at the bottom of pages
  navbar:
    logo: images/logo.png
    logo-alt: "Organization logo"   # alt text for the logo
  page-footer:
    left: "My Organization"
    center: "Questions? Email [me@example.gov](mailto:me@example.gov)"
    right: "Built with [Quarto](https://quarto.org)"
logo and logo-alt go under navbar:, not directly under website:.

title: Lesson 10: Customizing and accessibility
Lesson 10: Customizing and accessibility
section: Accessibility: make it usable for everyone
text:
Accessibility: make it usable for everyone
Public health sites should work for people using screen readers, keyboard navigation, or high contrast. Quarto handles much of this. You’re responsible for:







Check
How




Alt text on every image and chart
{fig-alt="..."} on images; #| fig-alt: on chunks


Meaningful link text
[Download the report](...), not [click here](...)


Headings in order
## then ###, without skipping levels; don’t use headings just to make text big


Readable contrast
Text must stand out from its background (at least 4.5:1). Some theme elements don’t, especially in dark mode. Check with a contrast tool, not by eye


Email addresses as links
[me@example.gov](mailto:me@example.gov)


Don’t rely on color alone
In charts, use labels or line styles as well as color









TipContrast fixes for cosmo and darkly



The NV OSE site’s styles.css contains tested fixes for some low-contrast parts of these two themes (buttons, previous/next links, code in headings). Copy it if you use the same themes.

title: Lesson 10: Customizing and accessibility
section: Copy buttons and table of contents
text:
Copy buttons and table of contents
format:
  html:
    toc: true                # "On this page" outline
    toc-title: "On this page"
    code-copy: true          # copy button on code blocks
    code-overflow: wrap      # wrap long code lines instead of scrolling

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
text: A website is a folder of .qmd pages plus a _quarto.yml file that ties them together with shared navigation, a theme, and search. Everything you learned about documents applies to each page.

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
text:
1. Create the project
Make the project inside your GitHub folder (e.g., Documents/GitHub/), so it’s easy to turn into a repo later.

PositronVS CodeRStudioTerminal



Open the Command Palette: Ctrl + Shift + P (Mac: Cmd + Shift + P).
Type and choose Quarto: Create Project.
Choose Website Project.
Pick the parent folder (e.g., Documents/GitHub) and type a name, like quarto-practice.
Positron opens the new project folder.




Open the Command Palette: Ctrl + Shift + P (Mac: Cmd + Shift + P).
Type and choose Quarto: Create Project.
Choose Website Project.
Pick the parent folder (e.g., Documents/GitHub) and type a name, like quarto-practice.
VS Code opens the new project folder.




File → New Project… → New Directory → Quarto Website.
Directory name: e.g., quarto-practice.
Create project as subdirectory of: click Browse and choose Documents/GitHub.
Leave the other options unchecked, and click Create Project.
RStudio opens the project and shows a Build tab.



Works with any editor:
cd ~/Documents/GitHub      # works in PowerShell, Git Bash, and Mac Terminal
quarto create project website quarto-practice
Then open the quarto-practice folder in your editor.

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
text:
2. What you get
quarto-practice/
├── _quarto.yml     ← site settings
├── index.qmd       ← home page
├── about.qmd       ← a second page
└── styles.css      ← custom styles (empty to start)

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
text:
3. _quarto.yml: the site’s control panel
Open _quarto.yml. A new project’s file looks roughly like this (comments added):
project:
  type: website          # this folder is a website

website:
  title: "quarto-practice"   # shown at the top left of every page
  navbar:                    # the bar across the top
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - about.qmd            # uses the page's own title as link text

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo             # the look (Lesson 10)
    css: styles.css
    toc: true                # "On this page" table of contents
Two changes to make right away:
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs           # ← add: put the rendered site in docs/ (for GitHub Pages)

website:
  title: "My Practice Site"  # ← change: a readable title
output-dir: docs matters in Lesson 11: GitHub Pages can publish straight from a docs/ folder.






WarningIndentation is meaning



In YAML, the number of spaces decides what belongs to what. navbar: is inside website: because it’s indented two spaces under it. Use two spaces per level, and never tabs. Most _quarto.yml errors are indentation mistakes.

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
text:
4. Add a page

Create a new file in the project folder, e.g., data-sources.qmd.
Give it a YAML header and some content:
---
title: "Data Sources"
---

## ESSENCE

Syndromic surveillance data from emergency departments.
Add it to the navbar in _quarto.yml:
website:
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - about.qmd
      - data-sources.qmd     # ← new

A page that isn’t in the navbar or sidebar still gets built, but nobody can find it unless something links to it.

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
section: 5. Organize pages in folders with a sidebar
text:
5. Organize pages in folders with a sidebar
For more than a handful of pages, put them in a folder and add a sidebar:
quarto-practice/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
└── lessons/
    ├── 01-intro.qmd
    ├── 02-data.qmd
    └── 03-charts.qmd
website:
  title: "My Practice Site"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: lessons/01-intro.qmd
        text: Lessons
  sidebar:
    style: docked
    contents:
      - section: "Lessons"
        contents:
          - lessons/01-intro.qmd
          - lessons/02-data.qmd
          - lessons/03-charts.qmd
Or let Quarto list every file in the folder automatically:
  sidebar:
    contents:
      - section: "Lessons"
        contents: "lessons/*"
Files are listed in alphabetical order, which is why lesson files are numbered: 01-, 02-, 03-.

More than one sidebar
A site with several sections (like this one, with one sidebar per training) gives each sidebar an id, and links the navbar to its first page. See the NV OSE site’s _quarto.yml for a working example.

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
text:
6. Linking between pages
Link to the .qmd file. Quarto turns it into the right .html link:
See [Lesson 2](02-data.qmd), or go back to the [home page](../index.qmd).
../ means “go up one folder.”

title: Lesson 8: Creating a website
section: 7. Add a navbar link to an outside site
text:
7. Add a navbar link to an outside site
website:
  navbar:
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/your-username/quarto-practice
        aria-label: "Source code on GitHub"
aria-label gives icon-only links a name for screen readers.

title: Lesson 6: Documents: HTML reports
text: A Quarto document is a single .qmd file that renders to a single output. The most flexible output is an HTML report: it opens in any web browser, can be emailed as one file, and supports everything from the previous lessons: tabs, collapsible callouts, and interactive tables.

title: Lesson 6: Documents: HTML reports
text:
1. Create a document

PositronVS CodeRStudio



File → New File… → Quarto Document, or create a file ending in .qmd.
Save it in a project folder, e.g., Documents/quarto-practice/ili-report.qmd.




Command Palette → Quarto: New Document, or create a file ending in .qmd.
Save it in a project folder, e.g., Documents/quarto-practice/ili-report.qmd.




File → New File → Quarto Document…
Enter a title, leave HTML selected, and click Create. (Uncheck “Use visual markdown editor” if you prefer source mode.)
Save it, e.g., ili-report.qmd.

title: Lesson 6: Documents: HTML reports
text:
2. A complete report
---
title: "Weekly ILI Summary"
subtitle: "Practice report with synthetic data"
author: "Jane Smith"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2026)
ili <- data.frame(
  week    = seq(as.Date("2025-09-28"), by = "week", length.out = 20),
  pct_ili = round(1.5 + 3 * exp(-((1:20 - 12)^2) / 18) + rnorm(20, 0, 0.2), 1)
)
peak <- ili[which.max(ili$pct_ili), ]
```

::: {.callout-note}
All data in this report is synthetic, for practice only.
:::

## Summary

ILI peaked at **`{r} peak$pct_ili`%** in the week of `{r} format(peak$week, "%B %d")`.

## Trend

```{r}
#| label: fig-trend
#| fig-cap: "Weekly percent of visits for ILI"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of weekly percent ILI over 20 weeks. It starts near
#|   1.5%, rises to a peak of about 4.5% around week 12, then falls back."
ggplot(ili, aes(week, pct_ili)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "% ILI")
```

@fig-trend shows the season so far.

## Data

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "Most recent five weeks"
knitr::kable(tail(ili, 5), col.names = c("Week", "% ILI"))
```
What’s happening:

date: today fills in the date when you render.
embed-resources: true packs images and styles into the one HTML file, so you can email it or put it on a shared drive and it still works.
echo: false hides the code for the whole report. Readers see results only.
The setup chunk loads packages and data without showing anything.
Inline code (`{r} peak$pct_ili`) writes the numbers into the sentence, so they always match the data.
@fig-trend becomes “Figure 1”, linked to the chart.

title: Lesson 6: Documents: HTML reports
text:
3. Render it

PositronVS CodeRStudioTerminal


Click Preview above the file, or press Ctrl + Shift + K. The report appears in the Viewer; the HTML file is saved next to the .qmd.


Click Preview above the file, or press Ctrl + Shift + K. The report opens in a side panel; the HTML file is saved next to the .qmd.


Click Render (or Ctrl + Shift + K). The report opens in the Viewer or a browser; the HTML file is saved next to the .qmd.


quarto render ili-report.qmd



The result is ili-report.html in the same folder. Double-click it to open it in your browser.

title: Lesson 6: Documents: HTML reports
text:
4. Useful HTML options
format:
  html:
    toc: true                  # table of contents
    toc-location: left         # ... on the left instead of the right
    number-sections: true      # 1, 1.1, 1.2 ...
    embed-resources: true      # one self-contained file
    code-fold: true            # code hidden behind "Show the code" buttons
    code-tools: true           # a menu to show/hide all code, or view the source
    df-print: paged            # data frames as scrollable, paged tables
    theme: flatly              # change the look (Lesson 10)
code-fold: true is a good middle ground for analysis write-ups: readers see results first, and can open the code if they want.

title: Lesson 6: Documents: HTML reports
text:
5. Reports that update themselves
The real power: change the data, render again, and the whole report updates: charts, tables, and every number in the text.
A typical routine report:

A setup chunk reads the newest data file.
Every number and chart is calculated from it.
Each week: drop in the new data, click Render, share the HTML.







ImportantReports with real data



An HTML report contains the results of your code (numbers, tables, charts), and with embed-resources: true the whole thing is in one file. Treat it like any other report with data: share it only through approved channels, and never publish it on a public site unless it’s cleared for release.

title: Lesson 6: Documents: HTML reports
text:
Other document formats
The same .qmd file can also render to Word (format: docx), PDF (format: pdf or format: typst), and more, by changing format: in the header. This training focuses on HTML. See Quarto’s Documents guide for the others.

title: Lesson 4: What Quarto adds to Markdown
text: Everything from Lesson 3 works in Quarto. This lesson covers what Quarto adds. None of this works on GitHub; it’s Quarto only.
crumbs: Lesson 4: What Quarto adds to Markdown

title: Lesson 4: What Quarto adds to Markdown
text:
1. The YAML header
Every .qmd file starts with a header between two --- lines. It’s written in YAML: key: value pairs that set up the document.
---
title: "Weekly ILI Summary"
subtitle: "Week 42, 2026"
author: "Jane Smith"
date: 2026-10-28
format: html
toc: true
---



Setting
What it does




title, subtitle, author, date
Shown at the top of the output


format
The type of output: html, revealjs (slides), and others (Lesson 6)


toc: true
Adds a table of contents


description

title: Troubleshooting
text: Common first-day problems, especially on Windows.

title: Troubleshooting
section: I don’t see R or Python icons
text:
I don’t see R or Python icons
That’s expected. Positron doesn’t put R or Python in the left sidebar. Start them from the interpreter picker in the top-right corner (Lesson 2).

title: Troubleshooting
section: How do I start a new R or Python console?
text:
How do I start a new R or Python console?

Top-right interpreter picker: choose an R or Python version. That starts a new session.
Console panel: click + (new session) at the top of the Console, or the dropdown arrow beside it, and choose R or Python.
Command Palette (Ctrl + Shift + P): type Interpreter: Start New Session.

To restart the current console instead, click ↻ at the top of the Console panel. You can have R and Python consoles open at the same time and switch between them at the top of the Console.

title: Troubleshooting
section: The interpreter picker shows no R or Python
text:
The interpreter picker shows no R or Python
Positron can’t find them on your computer. It doesn’t install them itself.

Install them: R from cran.r-project.org; Python from python.org (on Windows, check “Add python.exe to PATH”).
Restart Positron.
Still missing? Open the Command Palette (Ctrl + Shift + P) and run Interpreter: Discover all interpreters.
Check that Python is really installed (next section).

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Where is Python installed?

Windows: Command PromptWindows: PowerShellMac


where python
If you installed Python from python.org, the py launcher lists every installed version and its path:
py -0p


Get-Command python
or
where.exe python
In PowerShell, plain where means something else (Where-Object), so you need the .exe.


In Terminal:
which python3



You can also ask Python which executable it’s running from:
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
(On a Mac, use python3.)






WarningA path with WindowsApps in it



If the result is ...\WindowsApps\python.exe, that’s the Microsoft Store shortcut, not a real install, and it often fails in Positron. Install Python from python.org, check “Add python.exe to PATH”, restart Positron, and choose that version in the interpreter picker.

title: Troubleshooting
section: The Python Console is blank and I can’t type in it
text:
The Python Console is blank and I can’t type in it
The Python session usually hasn’t started or has crashed. Try these in order:

Wait. On first launch Python can take 10–30 seconds. If you see a spinner or “Starting…”, let it finish.
Restart the session: click ↻ at the top of the Console, or run Interpreter: Restart Active Interpreter from the Command Palette.
Check the logs: in the bottom panel, open the Output tab and choose Python Kernel or Python Language Pack from the dropdown on the right. Errors show up there.
Install ipykernel (the most common fix). In the Terminal tab, run:
python -m pip install ipykernel
Then restart Positron.
Check you have a real Python install, not the Microsoft Store shortcut (above).

title: Troubleshooting
section: I typed python in the Console and got an error
text:
I typed python in the Console and got an error
The Console is already running Python. Type the code itself, like print("hello"). Only the Terminal needs python first (Lesson 2).

title: Troubleshooting
section: I can’t see the Extensions panel
text:
I can’t see the Extensions panel

Press Ctrl + Shift + X to open the Extensions view.
If the whole icon bar on the left is missing: View → Appearance → Activity Bar Position → Default. Or search Activity Bar in the Command Palette.

title: Troubleshooting
section: My VS Code extensions aren’t here
text:
My VS Code extensions aren’t here
Positron is a separate app, so it doesn’t bring over VS Code extensions. It also installs from the Open VSX marketplace rather than Microsoft’s, so a few extensions (like Pylance and some other Microsoft ones) aren’t available.

In the Extensions view, search for each one and click Install.
If one isn’t listed, download its .vsix file, then in the Extensions view click ⋯ → Install from VSIX… and choose the file. Only install .vsix files from trusted sources.

Positron already includes R and Python support, so you don’t need separate extensions for them.

text:
I want dark mode
Ctrl + K, then Ctrl + T, and choose a dark theme (Lesson 2).

Exercise 5: Spot the problem (Lesson 9, 10 min, discussion)
Each of these is about to be committed. What’s wrong, and what should happen instead?
A.
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), server = "db-server.example.org",
                 uid = "jsmith", pwd = "Winter2026!")
B. A folder data/ containing measles_cases_2026.csv, with columns name, dob, zip, onset_date.
C. A colleague says: “I accidentally pushed my API key, but I deleted the file and pushed again, so it’s fine.”
D. A private repo with a summary table where one county has a count of 2.
E. .gitignore contains data/, but data/cases.csv still shows up on GitHub.






TipShow answers





A. It contains a password, a username, and an internal server name. Move the credentials to .Renviron or .env (ignored by Git) and use Sys.getenv(). Leave out the server name too, or keep it in config. If this was already pushed, change the password and tell an owner.
B. This is line-level PHI. It must never be on GitHub, public or private. Keep it on approved secure storage, add data/ to .gitignore, and use synthetic data for examples. If it was pushed, tell an owner and follow incident reporting procedures.
C. Not fine. The key is still in the history, and bots may already have it. Revoke the key right away, tell an owner, and clean the history.
D. Small cell counts can identify people. Follow the agency’s small-number suppression rules before sharing, even internally.
E. .gitignore doesn’t affect files that were already tracked. Run git rm --cached data/cases.csv and commit. The file remains in history, so treat it as exposed if it’s sensitive.

text:
ImportantThe most important lesson in this training



Git is designed to never forget. That’s great for code, and dangerous for data and secrets.

title: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub
section: Never commit any of these, in public or private repos
text:
Never commit any of these, in public or private repos

Data

❌ Protected health information (PHI): names, dates of birth, addresses, medical record numbers, case details
❌ Personally identifiable information (PII): Social Security numbers, phone numbers, email addresses of the public
❌ Line-level surveillance or case data, even if it’s “de-identified.” Small counts and combinations of fields (age + ZIP code + date) can identify people.
❌ Data covered by data use agreements (DUAs), IRB protocols, HIPAA, or state confidentiality rules
❌ Unreleased or provisional numbers that haven’t been cleared



Secrets (credentials)

❌ Passwords, including database and server passwords
❌ API keys and tokens, such as REDCap, Census, or cloud service keys, and GitHub tokens
❌ Usernames paired with systems, connection strings, and internal server names or IP addresses
❌ Private keys and certificates (.pem, .key, id_rsa)
❌ .env files and config files that contain any of the above



Also avoid

❌ Large files. GitHub warns at 50 MB and blocks files over 100 MB.
❌ Copyrighted material you don’t have rights to share
crumbs: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub

title: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub
text:
Why “just delete it” doesn’t work
When you commit a file, Git stores it permanently in the history. If you delete it and commit again:
Commit 1: Add analysis.R + patients.csv      ← patients.csv is still here
Commit 2: Delete patients.csv                ← only hidden from the latest version
Anyone with access can still:

open History, or run git log, and view the old commit
check out the old commit and get the file back
find it in every clone and fork made before you deleted it

And in a public repo:

Automated bots scan GitHub for leaked secrets within minutes of a push.
Search engines and archives may have already copied it.
Making the repo private, or deleting it, doesn’t undo copies that already exist.

Removing something from history completely requires rewriting the history (with tools like git filter-repo or BFG), force-pushing, getting everyone to re-clone, and sometimes contacting GitHub Support. It’s slow and error-prone, and never fully guaranteed. Prevention is much easier.
crumbs: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub

title: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub
section: How to keep secrets and data out
text:
How to keep secrets and data out

1. Set up .gitignore first
Before adding anything else to a new repo:
.env
*.key
*.pem
credentials*
config/secrets.*
data/raw/
data/confidential/
*.sas7bdat
*.xlsx
*.csv
You can add exceptions for safe files, for example !data/example/*.csv.


2. Keep secrets out of code
❌ Don’t do this:
con <- dbConnect(odbc(), uid = "jsmith", pwd = "Summer2026!")
api_key <- "a1b2c3d4e5f6"
✅ Do this instead. Store secrets in a file that Git ignores, or in your system’s environment variables.
R: put the values in your personal .Renviron file. In R, run file.edit("~/.Renviron") to open it. On Windows it’s usually in your Documents folder (C:\Users\<you>\Documents\.Renviron), outside any project, so it isn’t committed. If you ever keep one inside a project, add .Renviron to .gitignore.
# .Renviron (never committed)
DB_USER=jsmith
DB_PASS=Summer2026!
# analysis.R (safe to commit)
con <- dbConnect(odbc(),
                 uid = Sys.getenv("DB_USER"),
                 pwd = Sys.getenv("DB_PASS"))
Python: put the values in .env, and add .env to .gitignore.
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")
Even better, use your agency’s approved password manager or secrets tool.


3. Keep data out of the repo

Store real data on approved agency storage, such as secure network drives, and point your code to it.
Commit code, not data. Document in the README where authorized users can find the data.
For examples and training, use synthetic (fake) data or public, aggregated datasets.



4. Review before every commit

In GitHub Desktop, look at every file and line in the Changes tab.
On the command line, run git status and git diff --staged before committing.
Ask yourself: Would I be comfortable if this were on the front page of the news?



5. Let GitHub help

Push protection blocks many known secret formats, such as API keys and tokens. NV OSE has it turned on for public repos. Turn it on for your own account too: Settings → Code security → Push protection for yourself.
Don’t rely on it alone. It doesn’t detect PHI or data, and it doesn’t catch every kind of password.
crumbs: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub

title: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub
text:
If something sensitive is committed
Act quickly, and don’t try to hide it.

Don’t push, if you haven’t yet. Undo the commit: in GitHub Desktop, History → Undo commit; on the command line, git reset --soft HEAD~1. Then remove the file and add it to .gitignore.
If it’s already pushed:

Tell an NV OSE owner immediately: Max Wegener (mwegener@health.nv.gov) or Jordan Lancaster (jlancaster@health.nv.gov).
Secrets: revoke or change them right away. Treat the password or token as compromised, even if the repo is private or you deleted it quickly.
Data (PHI/PII): follow the agency’s privacy and security incident reporting procedures. This may be a reportable breach.

An owner will help remove it from history and check forks and clones.
crumbs: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub

title: Lesson 9: Data security: what never goes on GitHub
text:
Quick self-check
Before you push, ask:

Did I check every changed file?
Is there any real data, or anything that could identify a person?
Is there any password, token, key, username, or server name?
Is my .gitignore covering data and secret files?
If this repo is public, is everything in it cleared for public release?

title: Lesson 7: Clones, forks, and templates
text:
Fork
A fork is your own copy of someone else’s project, on GitHub.

On the repo’s page, click Fork (top right) → Create fork.
Clone your fork to your computer and make changes.
To suggest your changes to the original project, open a pull request from your fork.
To get the original’s newest changes, click Sync fork on your fork’s page.


When to fork, and when to use a branch

Inside NV OSE: use branches, not forks. You already have access.
Outside projects (another agency’s or an open-source package): fork.



Fork rules to know

A fork of a public repo is public.
A fork of a private repo stays private, and NV OSE has turned off forking of its private repos.
If a public repo is deleted or made private, existing public forks remain. This is one more reason never to put sensitive data in a public repo (see Lesson 9).

A template repo has a Use this template button. Clicking it creates a brand-new repo with the same files but none of the history. It’s great for standard project setups.
The GitHub Skills course Introduction to GitHub uses a template. Try it for extra hands-on practice.

title: Lesson 3: Repositories, READMEs, and .gitignore
text:
.gitignore
A .gitignore file tells Git which files to never track. It’s one of your most important safety tools.
# Operating-system clutter
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# R
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user/

# Python
__pycache__/
.venv/

# Secrets: NEVER commit these
.env
*.key
credentials.json

# Data: keep real data out of Git
data/raw/
*.sas7bdat
*.xlsx

How it works

Each line is a pattern. * matches anything, a trailing / means a folder, and # starts a comment.
Ignored files stay on your computer. Git just doesn’t track them or upload them.
GitHub has ready-made templates in the github/gitignore repo.



Gotcha: .gitignore doesn’t affect files already tracked
If a file was committed before you added it to .gitignore, Git keeps tracking it. To stop tracking it, but keep it on your computer:
git rm --cached path/to/file
git commit -m "Stop tracking file"
The file still exists in earlier commits. If it contained sensitive information, see Lesson 9.






TipBest practice



Create the .gitignore first, before you add any data or secrets to the folder.

title: Lesson 1: Git vs. GitHub: what and why
text:
Most of us have a folder that looks like this:
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_v2.R
analysis_final_v2_JL_edits.R
analysis_FINAL_actually_final.R
Version control replaces that with one file and a complete, labeled history of every change: who changed what, when, and why. You can go back to any earlier version at any time.
For public health work, this means:

Reproducibility. You can show exactly which code produced a report.
Collaboration. Several people can work on the same project without emailing files or overwriting each other.
Continuity. When someone leaves, their work and its history stay with the team.
Safety. Mistakes can be undone.

Git vs. GitHub









Git
GitHub




What it is
Version control software
A website that hosts Git repositories


Where it runs
On your computer
In the cloud (github.com)


Needs internet?
No
Yes


What it does
Tracks changes to files in a folder

Made by
Linus Torvalds (2005), open source
GitHub, Inc. (owned by Microsoft)

 Your computer (local)                              GitHub (remote)

title: Lesson 6: Branches and pull requests
text:
A branch is a separate copy of the project where you can make changes without affecting the main version. When the work is ready, you merge it back.
main:      A───B───────────E (merge)
                \         /
my-branch:       C───D───┘

main is the official, working version.
You create my-branch, make commits C and D, and main is unaffected.
When you’re done, you merge the branch back into main.

Why use branches? You can experiment safely, several people can work at once, and every change can be reviewed before it reaches main. The NV OSE SOP requires this for shared repos.
Naming: yourname/short-description, for example mwegener/add-age-filter.

title: Lesson 6: Branches and pull requests
text:
The branch → PR → merge workflow

In GitHub Desktop

Current branch → New branch. Name it, and base it on main.
Make your changes, then Commit to your-branch.
Click Publish branch. This pushes the branch to GitHub.
Click Create Pull Request. Your browser opens on GitHub.
Add a title and description, choose Reviewers on the right, then click Create pull request.
After approval, click Merge pull request on GitHub, then Delete branch.
Back in Desktop, switch to main and click Pull origin.



On the command line
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c mwegener/add-age-filter      # Create and switch to a new branch
# ... edit, then:
git add .
git commit -m "Add age filter"
git push -u origin mwegener/add-age-filter
Then open the PR on github.com. GitHub shows a yellow Compare & pull request banner. After it’s merged:
git switch main
git pull
git branch -d mwegener/add-age-filter      # Delete the local branch
Other branch commands:
git branch               # List local branches (* marks the current one)
git branch -a            # Include branches on GitHub
git switch branch-name   # Switch to an existing branch

title: Lesson 6: Branches and pull requests
text:
Reviewing a pull request

Open the PR and go to the Files changed tab.
Click + next to a line to comment on it.
Click Review changes and choose Comment, Approve, or Request changes.

When reviewing, ask: Does it work? Is it clear? Is there any sensitive data or any credential in it?

title: Lesson 6: Branches and pull requests
text:
Merge conflicts
A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines of the same file. Git can’t decide which version to keep, so it asks you.
The file will contain markers like this:
<<<<<<< HEAD
age_groups <- c("0-17", "18-64", "65+")
=======
age_groups <- c("0-4", "5-17", "18-49", "50-64", "65+")
>>>>>>> mwegener/add-age-filter
To resolve it:

Edit the file so it contains the version you want, and delete all of the marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>).
Save the file, then stage and commit it. GitHub Desktop walks you through this, and GitHub can resolve simple conflicts in the browser.

To avoid conflicts: pull often, keep branches short-lived, and talk with your team about who is editing what.

title: Glossary
text:
Term
Definition




Branch
A separate line of development. main is the default branch.


Clone
A full copy of a repo, including its history, on your computer.


Commit
A saved snapshot of changes, with a message, an author, and a unique ID (hash).


Commit message
A short description of what a commit changed and why.


Conflict (merge conflict)
When two changes affect the same lines and Git needs you to choose which to keep.


Diff
The line-by-line difference between two versions of a file.


Fetch
Check GitHub for new changes without applying them.


Fork
Your own copy of someone else’s repo on GitHub.


.gitignore
A file listing patterns for files Git should never track.


GitHub Pages
A free GitHub service that turns a repo into a website.


HEAD
The commit you are currently on.


Issue
A GitHub item for tracking a task, bug, or idea.


Local
Your computer’s copy of a repo.


main
The default, official branch of a repo.


Markdown (.md)
A simple text formatting language used for READMEs and documentation.


Merge
Combine the changes from one branch into another.


Organization (org)
A shared GitHub account for a team, such as nv-ose.


origin
The default name for the remote copy of the repo on GitHub.


Owner
An org member with full admin rights.


Pull
Fetch new changes from GitHub and merge them into your local copy.


Pull request (PR)
A request to merge one branch into another, with review and discussion.


Push
Upload your local commits to GitHub.


Push protection
A GitHub feature that blocks pushes containing known secret formats.


README
The front-page document of a repo, usually README.md.


Remote
A copy of the repo hosted elsewhere, usually on GitHub.


Repository (repo)
A project folder tracked by Git, plus its history.


Revert
A new commit that undoes an earlier commit.


Secret
Any credential: a password, API key, token, or private key.


Stage (staging area)
The set of changes chosen to go into the next commit (git add).


Template repository
A repo you can use to start new repos with the same files, without its history.


Two-factor authentication (2FA)
A second login step, such as an app code, that protects your account.

title: Writing a good README
text:
A README is a short document that explains a project: what it is, how to use it, and who to ask. Every NV OSE repository needs one, and most project folders benefit from one even if they never go on GitHub.
⬇ Download the NV OSE README template

title: Writing a good README
text:
Why READMEs matter

It’s the front page. GitHub shows README.md automatically below a repo’s file list. It’s the first thing anyone sees.
Handoffs. When someone leaves, goes on leave, or covers for a colleague, the README is how the next person runs the project.
Future you. In six months you won’t remember which script runs first or where the data lives.
Findability. A clear first sentence tells people, in search results and in the member directory, whether this is the project they need.
Fewer questions. Setup steps and a troubleshooting table answer the most common questions before anyone has to ask.

title: Writing a good README
text:
Tips

Lead with the one-line description. “Weekly data pipeline for the Nevada Respiratory Surveillance Dashboard” beats “This repo contains scripts.”
Write for someone new. Assume they know R but not your project.
Show the run order. Number scripts (01_import.R, 02_clean.R) and list them in order.
Say where data lives, never include it. “Line list is on the S: drive in Respiratory/2026/” is fine. The data itself, or a path with a username in it, is not.
List systems, never credentials. “Needs a REDCap API token in ~/.Renviron,” never the token.
Use relative links to files in the repo: [the report](notebooks/report.qmd).
Keep it current. Update the README in the same commit as the change it describes. A wrong README is worse than none.
Use headings, tables, and short lists. People scan READMEs; they don’t read them top to bottom.

No. RStudio is still supported, and everything in your R projects keeps working in both. Many people use Positron for new projects, or for anything that mixes R and Python.

Creating a new project from a template
Positron can create a new project folder for you: File → New Folder from Template…


Choose R Project (or Python Project), and click Next.
Enter a Folder Name (lowercase, hyphens: my-r-project) and choose its Location, such as your Documents\GitHub folder.

title: Lesson 3: Projects: folders, not .Rproj
text:
The .here file and here::here()
Scripts need file paths, like raw_data/cases.csv. Typing full paths (C:\Users\...) breaks as soon as someone else runs your code, or the folder moves. The here package fixes this by building every path from the project’s top folder:
library(here)
cases <- read.csv(here("raw_data", "cases.csv"))
here() finds the top folder by looking for a marker file. An empty file called .here is the clearest marker. Create one once per project. In the Console, with your project open:
install.packages("here")   # first time only
here::set_here()           # creates an empty .here file in the current folder
Or create it in the Explorer: a new file named .here (Lesson 4).
Check it works:
here::here()

here() returns your project’s top folder. From now on, here("raw_data", "cases.csv") works for anyone, wherever the folder is saved.






Tip



here() also recognizes an .Rproj file or a .git folder as the top of a project, but a .here file is the most reliable, and it works the same in Positron, RStudio, and VS Code.

title: Lesson 1: What is Quarto?
text:
Quarto builds on Markdown
Quarto is free, open-source software from Posit (the company behind RStudio) that takes Markdown much further. You write a .qmd file (“Quarto Markdown”), and Quarto renders it into a finished product:
            ┌──────────────┐
            │              ├──► report.html  (web page / report)
 file.qmd ──►    Quarto    ├──► slides.html  (presentation)
 (Markdown  │  (+ R runs   ├──► a website    (many linked pages)
  + R code) │  your code)  ├──► .docx, .pdf  (Word, PDF)
            └──────────────┘

What Quarto adds







Plain Markdown
Quarto




Formatting only
Formatting plus running R, Python, or Julia code and inserting the results


One output: a formatted page
Many outputs from the same file: HTML, slides, websites, Word, PDF, and more


No settings
A YAML header to set the title, author, theme, table of contents, and more


Basic elements
Callout boxes, tabs, columns, cross-referenced figures and tables, footnotes, citations


You style it however your app styles it
Built-in themes, light and dark mode, accessible defaults





Quarto and R Markdown
If you’ve used R Markdown (.Rmd files), Quarto is its successor. The ideas are the same, but Quarto works with more languages and editors, and most .Rmd files render in Quarto with few or no changes.

text:
What people use Quarto for







Use
Example in public health




Reports
A weekly surveillance summary where the charts and numbers update from the data automatically


Presentations
Conference talks and briefings with live charts and code, as a web-based slide deck


Websites
Training sites (like this one), project documentation, a team’s resource hub


Documentation
A pipeline’s how-to guide, like a step-by-step report.qmd that staff run each week


Books and manuals
A multi-chapter methods manual or SOP


Dashboards
A simple page of charts and value boxes



The Quarto Gallery has hundreds of examples.

Why it’s worth learning

Reproducible. The chart in the report is produced by the code beside it. Rerun with new data, and everything updates, with no copy-pasting from R into Word.
One skill, many outputs. The same Markdown and code make reports, slides, and websites.
Plain text. Files are small, readable, and version-controlled with Git.
Free. Quarto is free, and so is publishing on GitHub Pages.

title: Lesson 5: Code in Quarto
text: This is what makes Quarto different from Markdown: it can run your R code and put the results (tables, charts, numbers) into the document.

title: Lesson 5: Code in Quarto
text:
Code chunks
A code chunk looks like a Markdown code block, but with the language in curly braces: {r}. Quarto runs it.
```{r}
cases <- data.frame(
  county = c("Clark", "Washoe", "Carson City"),
  cases  = c(120, 45, 8)
)
cases
```
When rendered, the output shows the code, then the result printed below it.

PositronVS CodeRStudio



Insert a chunk: Command Palette → Quarto: Insert Code Cell, or type it by hand.
Run one chunk while you write: click Run Cell above it, or Ctrl + Shift + Enter.




Insert a chunk: Command Palette → Quarto: Insert Code Cell, or type it by hand.
Run one chunk while you write: click Run Cell above it, or Ctrl + Shift + Enter.




Insert a chunk: Ctrl + Alt + I (Mac: Cmd + Option + I), or the green +C button.
Run one chunk while you write: click the green ▶ at its top right, or Ctrl + Shift + Enter.




Running a chunk by hand only runs it in your R session. Rendering runs every chunk, from top to bottom, in a fresh session, so every chunk must work in order.

title: Lesson 5: Code in Quarto
text:
Chunk options
Options go at the top of a chunk, each on its own line starting with #|:
```{r}
#| label: fig-ili
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Weekly percent of visits for influenza-like illness"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of weekly percent ILI over 20 weeks, rising from
#|   about 1.5% to a peak near 4.5% in week 12, then falling."

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(ili, aes(week, pct_ili)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "% ILI")
```
Common options:







Option
What it does




label: name
Names the chunk (no spaces). A label starting with fig- makes a numbered figure you can cross-reference


echo: false
Hide the code; show only the result


eval: false
Show the code, but don’t run it


include: false
Run the code, but show nothing (good for loading packages and data)


warning: false / message: false
Hide warnings / messages


fig-alt: "..."
Alt text for a chart (required for every chart)


fig-cap: "..."
Visible caption


fig-width, fig-height
Chart size, in inches




Options for the whole document
Set defaults for every chunk in the YAML header:
---
title: "Weekly ILI Summary"
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---
A typical report sets echo: false, so readers see results, not code. A training or tutorial leaves code visible.

title: Lesson 5: Code in Quarto
text:
Inline code
Put a result inside a sentence with `{r} expression`:
This week there were `{r} sum(cases$cases)` cases across
`{r} nrow(cases)` counties.
When rendered: “This week there were 173 cases across 3 counties.” Numbers in the text always match the data.

```{r}

```

text:
A typical setup chunk
Most documents start with one hidden chunk that loads packages and data:
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
cases <- read_csv("data/example_cases.csv")
```

title: Lesson 5: Code in Quarto
section: Freeze: don’t re-run everything every time
text:
Freeze: don’t re-run everything every time
In a project with many pages (like a website), you can tell Quarto to save results and only re-run a page’s code when that code changes:
# in _quarto.yml
execute:
  freeze: auto
The saved results go in a _freeze/ folder. Commit it with the rest of the project (Lesson 9).






ImportantReal data never goes in published output



Code runs when you render, and its results are written into the output. Anything you share or publish (a report, slides, a website) must use made-up (synthetic) or public data, unless it’s cleared for release. Never put passwords or API keys in a .qmd file. See Data security.

title: Lesson 7: Presentations with revealjs
text: Quarto makes slide presentations from the same Markdown and R code. The main slide format is revealjs: slides that run in a web browser, so they work on any computer, can include live code results, and can be shared as a single file or a link.

1. Your first deck
Create a file, e.g., talk.qmd:
---
title: "Influenza Season Update"
subtitle: "Practice deck with synthetic data"
author: "Jane Smith"
date: today
format: revealjs
---

## Where we are

- ILI is rising in most counties
- Peak expected in about 3 weeks
- Vaccination clinics continue through December

## Next steps

Coordinate with local health authorities on clinic hours.

format: revealjs makes it a slide deck.
The title, subtitle, author, and date become the title slide.
Every ## heading starts a new slide.

Render it the same way as a document (Preview or Ctrl + Shift + K). The output is talk.html; open it in a browser to present.

2. Slides without titles, and sections
## Slide with a title

Content

---

This slide has no title. Three dashes start a new slide.

# Part 2: Data

## The next slide
A single # heading makes a section title slide, and the ## slides after it are stacked vertically under that section (you move through them with ↓). If you’d rather keep every slide in one left-to-right line, use only ##.

3. Revealing content step by step

::: {.incremental}
- Cases up 20% from last week
- Highest rates in children under 5
- Hospitalizations stable
:::

## A pause

First this appears.

. . .

Then this, on the next click.
To make every list in the deck appear item by item, add incremental: true under revealjs: in the header.

5. Speaker notes

Coordinate with local health authorities.

::: {.notes}
Mention the December clinic schedule. Pause for questions.
:::
Notes don’t appear on the slides. Press S while presenting to open the speaker view, with your notes, a timer, and the next slide.

title: Lesson 7: Presentations with revealjs
text:
6. Charts and code on slides
R chunks work on slides exactly as in documents:
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of weekly percent ILI rising to a peak near 4.5% in week 12."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(ili, aes(week, pct_ili)) + geom_line() + labs(x = "Week", y = "% ILI")
```
Usually you’ll hide the code (echo: false) and show only the chart. For a coding talk, show it, and highlight lines in order with code-line-numbers: "1|2-3".

title: Lesson 7: Presentations with revealjs
text:
7. Settings for the whole deck
---
title: "Influenza Season Update"
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: simple            # also: default, dark, serif, solarized, moon, ...
    slide-number: true       # number in the corner
    incremental: false       # true = all lists appear item by item
    footer: "NV OSE | Synthetic data"
    logo: images/logo.png
    embed-resources: true    # one self-contained HTML file
execute:
  echo: false
---
embed-resources: true makes the deck a single file you can email, put on a shared drive, or upload to a training site, and it still works offline.

title: Lesson 7: Presentations with revealjs
text:
8. Presenting
Open the HTML file in a browser, then:



Key
Does

←

text:
9. Accessibility on slides

Alt text on every image and chart (fig-alt), exactly as in documents.
Keep text short and large; don’t cram slides.
Check contrast, especially with dark themes and colored text.
Don’t rely on color alone in charts.







TipNeed PowerPoint?



If someone requires a .pptx file, Quarto can also render format: pptx. Fewer features work (no incremental reveals or interactive output), but the content carries over. See Quarto’s PowerPoint guide.

title: Lesson 9: Previewing, rendering, and fixing errors
text:
Preview
Render

text:
Pages with R code: freeze
When you render, Quarto runs the R code on every page. That can be slow, and anyone who renders the site needs every R package used.
Freeze saves the results, so code only re-runs when that page’s code changes:
# in _quarto.yml
execute:
  freeze: auto
Quarto stores the saved results in a _freeze/ folder. Commit _freeze/ along with docs/.
If a page’s code needs passwords, internal servers, or real data, it shouldn’t run on a website at all. Use eval: false to show it without running it, and never publish its output.

Common errors and fixes



Error message contains…
Likely cause
Fix




YAML parse error / bad indentation
A spacing mistake in _quarto.yml or a page header
Check indentation (two spaces per level, no tabs) and the space after each colon


property name ... is invalid
A setting in the wrong place (e.g., logo: under website: instead of navbar:)
Check the Quarto reference for where the setting goes


there is no package called 'ggplot2'
An R package isn’t installed
install.packages("ggplot2")


R installation not found / knitr not found
Quarto can’t find R, or knitr isn’t installed
Run quarto check; install rmarkdown and knitr; restart the editor


Error in ... : object 'x' not found (with a chunk name)
The R code has an error
Run that chunk in R to debug. The message tells you which chunk failed


Unable to resolve link target (warning)
A link points to a file that doesn’t exist
Fix the path or file name


A page is missing from the site
It’s not in the navbar/sidebar, or not in a render: list
Add it to _quarto.yml









Tip



Read the first error message. Later messages are often just consequences of the first one.

title: Lesson 11: Publishing on GitHub Pages
section: The approach: render to docs/, publish from docs/
text:
The approach: render to docs/, publish from docs/
There are several ways to publish a Quarto site. This training (and the NV OSE site) uses the simplest one: commit the rendered site in a docs/ folder, and tell GitHub Pages to serve that folder. It works with GitHub Desktop and needs no extra setup.

Step 1: Prepare the project
In _quarto.yml:
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
In the project folder, create an empty file named .nojekyll (with the dot). It tells GitHub Pages to serve your files as they are, instead of processing them with its own site builder (Jekyll), which can break Quarto sites. To copy it into docs/ on every render, add:
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
  resources:
    - "/.nojekyll"
The easiest way is from the terminal, in the project folder. The command depends on which terminal you’re using:







Terminal
Command




PowerShell (the default terminal in Positron and VS Code on Windows)
New-Item .nojekyll


Command Prompt (cmd)
type nul > .nojekyll


Git Bash, or Terminal on a Mac
touch .nojekyll



Not sure which one you have? In Positron and VS Code, the terminal’s name (e.g., powershell) is shown at the top right of the Terminal panel. In RStudio, check Tools → Global Options → Terminal.


Step 2: Render
quarto render
Check that docs/ contains index.html and .nojekyll.


Step 3: Make sure docs/ isn’t ignored
GitHub only publishes files you commit. Open .gitignore (if there is one) and make sure it doesn’t contain docs/. Do ignore Quarto’s cache:
/.quarto/


Step 4: Put the project on GitHub
In GitHub Desktop (see the Git and GitHub training):

File → Add local repository, choose the project folder, then click create a repository.
Check the Changes list: your .qmd files, _quarto.yml, styles.css, and everything in docs/. Commit.
Click Publish repository. For a practice site, use your personal account and uncheck Keep this code private (Pages needs a public repo). For NV OSE, choose the nv-ose organization, and ask an owner before making anything public.



Step 5: Turn on GitHub Pages

On github.com, open the repo and go to Settings → Pages.
Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch.
Set Branch to main and the folder to /docs. Click Save.
Wait 1–2 minutes and refresh. The page shows “Your site is live at …” with the address.







Tip



On the repo’s main page, click ⚙️ next to About and check Use your GitHub Pages website, so the site link appears on the repo.

title: Lesson 11: Publishing on GitHub Pages
text:
Updating the site
Every change follows the same loop:
edit .qmd ──► quarto render ──► commit (including docs/) ──► push ──► live in 1–2 min






ImportantThe most common mistake



Editing a .qmd file and pushing without rendering. The source changes, but docs/ doesn’t, so the live site stays the same. If your change isn’t showing up, render, then commit the docs/ changes.


If the site still looks old after a few minutes:

Do a hard refresh: Ctrl + Shift + R (Mac: Cmd + Shift + R).
Check the repo’s Actions tab. The pages build and deployment run should have a green ✅. A red ❌ shows an error message.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text: Learn to write with Markdown, turn text and R code into reports and slides with Quarto, and publish a website on GitHub Pages. This is how the NV OSE training site you’re reading right now is built.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Overview

Audience: Anyone who writes reports, presentations, documentation, or trainings, especially if you use R
Level: Beginner (no Markdown or Quarto experience needed)
Duration: About 5 hours, in three sessions (below)
Format: Workshop or self-paced
Editors: Instructions for Positron, VS Code, and RStudio. Pick your editor once in any tab set, and every page follows your choice.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this training, you will be able to:

Write formatted text in Markdown, and explain what Quarto adds to it.
Describe what Quarto is used for, and install it.
Add callouts, tabs, figures with alt text, and R code chunks to a Quarto document.
Create an HTML report that combines text, code, tables, and charts.
Build a slide presentation with revealjs.
Create a website, publish it on GitHub Pages, and keep it updated.
Make your Quarto outputs accessible.
Add a new training to the NV OSE training site.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Prerequisites

Session 1: none. Install Quarto, R, and an editor (Positron, VS Code, or RStudio) as part of Lesson 2.
New to Positron? The 45-minute Introduction to Positron covers the editor first.
Session 3 (publishing): a GitHub account and GitHub Desktop. The Introduction to Git and GitHub training first is recommended.

Basic R helps but isn’t required. The code examples are short and explained.






Note



On a state computer you may need IT to install Quarto, R, or an editor. Request them ahead of time.
